title: Flux vs Flux Density: Weber, Tesla and When They Are Not the Same
h1: Magnetic flux vs flux density — weber and tesla explained
description: Flux (Wb) is total field through a surface; flux density (T) is field per unit area. 1 T = 1 Wb/m². Confusing them mis-sizes transformer cores.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Φ = B × A. A 1 T field through 100 cm² gives 0.01 Wb. Transformer core loss scales with B, not Φ.
body: The two most common magnetic units answer different questions. Flux is a total; flux density is an intensity. Which one you need depends on whether you are computing an EMF or a saturation limit.

> Φ (weber) = B (tesla) × A (m²)
> 1 T = 1 Wb/m² = 10 000 G = 10⁸ Mx/cm² (maxwell per cm²)

Flux (Wb): induced EMF (Faraday: V = -dΦ/dt), coil linkage, transformer core specification. Flux density (T): saturation limits, motor air-gap fields, MRI strength, magnetic force per area (Maxwell stress).

A 240 V, 50 Hz primary with 500 turns needs peak flux Φ = V/(4.44 fN) = 240/(4.44 × 50 × 500) = 2.16 mWb. In a 6 cm² core cross-section, B_peak = 2.16 × 10⁻³ / 6 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.6 T — well above silicon-steel saturation (~2.0 T). Either add turns or grow the core.
Flux is total; density is per area. Sizing cores lives in T; induced voltage lives in Wb.

faqs.a: In legacy US datasheets and NDT, yes. 1 Wb = 10⁸ Mx. Modern engineering uses weber.
λ = NΦ — the flux threading a coil times the number of turns. It appears directly in inductance L = λ/i.
